title: Osso Buco
subtitle: Milanese braised veal shin with gremolata
excerpt: The great Milanese braise: thick cross-sections of veal shin cooked low and slow in white wine, stock, and aromatic vegetables until the meat is falling from the bone and the marrow in the hollow of the shin is soft and rich. Finished with fresh gremolata.

recipe.sourceNotes: Osso buco (hollow bone) is the signature dish of Milanese cooking: cross-cut sections of veal shin braised in white wine and stock until the connective tissue and collagen have dissolved into a thick, gelatinous sauce. The marrow in the hollow of the bone is considered a delicacy and is eaten with a small spoon. The dish is finished with gremolata, the condiment of finely chopped lemon zest, garlic, and parsley that is scattered over at the last moment to brighten the rich braise with citrus and freshness. Osso buco alla milanese is traditionally served with saffron risotto (risotto alla milanese), making a meal that is among the great combinations in Italian cooking. The modern version uses tomatoes; the older bianco version does not.

content.text: Tie a piece of kitchen string around each veal shin cross-section to hold the meat together during braising; the connective tissue shrinks as it cooks and can push the meat out of shape. Brown the meat deeply on all sides before braising: colour equals flavour. The braise should barely tremble; hard bubbling toughens the meat and breaks the shin apart before the collagen has dissolved.

items.preparation: cross-cut sections (osso buco cuts), about 4 cm thick; tied with string

content.text: Season the veal portions and dust lightly in flour, shaking off the excess. Heat the olive oil and butter in a wide casserole over high heat. Brown the veal deeply on all sides, about 4 minutes per side. Remove and set aside. Reduce to medium heat. Fry the onion, carrot, and celery for 10 minutes until soft and lightly golden.

Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up any browned bits. Add the stock, tinned tomatoes, bay leaves, and thyme. Return the veal to the pan; the liquid should come about halfway up the sides of the meat. Bring to a gentle simmer.

Cover and braise over very low heat for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours, turning the meat once halfway through, until the meat is very tender and pulling away from the bone. Remove the string. Meanwhile, mix the gremolata: combine the lemon zest, grated garlic, and chopped parsley. Serve each shin with sauce spooned over and gremolata scattered on top.
